fixes.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Peter says the scoffers will ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” I think it sounds like someone staring at the oven and asking “Is it done yet?” every thirty seconds. Peter says scoffers like that will come in the last days, and he wants believers ready for them.

Exactly. The scoffers say, “…everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.” They say it right after asking where the promise of His coming is. Peter doesn't go along with them, and he's about to say why.

That's not what the scoffers say, friend. They say everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation. Changes is the opposite of that. Peter spends the next verses answering what they say.

That's it, baker. Peter says the world of that time perished in the flood. He ties it to water: the earth was formed out of water and by water, and the world of that time perished through that same water. Peter says the scoffers deliberately overlook this when they say everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation (2 Peter 3:4-6).

Hold on, baker, nobody's rationing cookies in this verse. Peter points to water, the same water the earth was formed out of and by. Through it, he says, the world of that time perished in the flood. That's the answer.

Peter doesn't compare a day to a breath, baker. He says, “With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.” He gives it both ways, and a breath isn't in either one. That's the one thing he doesn't want escaping their notice (2 Peter 3:8).
Angry isn't Peter's word, baker. He says the Lord “…is patient with you…” and that “you” matters. The patience is aimed at the very people he's writing to. Not slow, not angry, patient.

Offerings aren't in this verse, friend. Peter says the Lord is “…not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.” That's what the patience is about here. Nobody is left out of that "everyone" (2 Peter 3:9).

That's a lovely thought, friend, but Peter doesn't say it. He says, “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth…” The promise is God's, and what it points to is a new heaven and a new earth. Eden isn't named in this verse (2 Peter 3:13).

No temple in this verse, baker. After all that talk of fire, Peter turns with a “But” and says, “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth…” That one little word flips the mood, like the oven timer finally going off. The new heaven and new earth are what he names (2 Peter 3:13).

Sorrow isn't in this verse, friend. Peter says the new heaven and new earth are a place “…where righteousness dwells.” Dwells means it lives there, like it's home. So what he names is righteousness, not sorrow (2 Peter 3:13).
Silence does sound peaceful, baker, but Peter doesn't go there. He says “…where righteousness dwells.” After all that fire and melting, that's the thing he says lives in the new place (2 Peter 3:13).

Delay is a fair-sounding word, friend, but Peter doesn't say it. He says, “Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation…” Earlier he said the Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness (2 Peter 3:9). So where some see slowness, Peter points to salvation.

Doubt isn't where Peter lands, baker. He says, “Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation…” He's telling them to look at the waiting again, because it leads somewhere good. That's a long way from doubt.

Family favor isn't in this verse, baker. Peter's worry is that the error of the lawless could carry them away. What they could fall from is their secure standing. That's why he says to be on guard (2 Peter 3:17).
